papers.title: Governed Hybrid Agency: A Critical Evidence Map of Cognitive Architectures for Foundation-Model Agents
papers.summary: Background. Cognitive architectures specify the persistent memories, representations, learning processes, and control loops that allow an artificial agent to remain coherent across tasks and time. Foundation models provide broad generative competence, but do not by themselves ensure grounded action, reliable long-horizon memory, calibrated uncertainty, execution monitoring, or accountable learning. Objectives. This critical integrative review examines how cognitive-architecture principles are being used to govern foundation-model agents. Taking the last comprehensive pre-foundation-model survey of cognitive architectures (Kotseruba & Tsotsos, first published online in 2018) as its historical baseline, it maps developments across twelve ability channels, identifies recurring integration patterns, and derives testable design and evaluation requirements. Methods. We combined a historical-theoretical synthesis with a focused, PRISMA-informed evidence map of English-language records indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, searched in July 2026 over the 2018–2026 window. Queries required terms for cognitive architectures or architecture-level cognitive systems, foundation or generative models, and governance-relevant mechanisms. The searches identified 1,173 records; after deduplication, rule-based filtering, and LLMassisted title-and-abstract assessment, 119 works

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted HPLC Method Development and Optimization: A Review
papers.summary: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) continues to be the primary tool in pharmaceutical, environmental, food, and bioanalytical laboratories; however, creating a reliable method is still a gradual, repetitive, and skill-dependent process. Traditional approaches reliant on analyst expertise, sequential one-factor screening, retention modelling, and statistical design of experiments (DoE) are efficient but become ineffective as the number of essential technique parameters, analyte categories, or column chemistries increases. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing traditional machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), Bayesian optimisation, and reinforcement learning (RL), is currently utilised at every phase of method development: forecasting retention behaviour based on molecular structure, choosing columns and mobile phases, refining gradients, and progressively directing automated experimentation. This critique encapsulates the principles of HPLC method formulation, delineates the primary AI frameworks and their chromatographic utilisations, juxtaposes retention-time forecasting models and optimisation techniques in a tabular format, explores the synergy with analytical quality by design (AQbD) and the ICH Q14 and Q2(R2) guidelines, and rigorously assesses constraints including data insufficiency, inadequate transferability across systems, absence of interpretabil

papers.title: From Code Completion to Agentic Development: A Survey of AI Coding Agents, Ecosystems, and Evolving Software Engineering Practice
papers.summary: Abstract Large language models have extended software-development assistance from token-level completion to systems that can navigate repositories, edit files, execute tools, and iterate on test feedback. This survey studies the design, use, and evaluation of these AI coding agents, together with their commercial and societal context. Reproducible database queries support literature discovery, but the cited corpus is selected and coded for relevance; we therefore describe the work as a structured scoping survey rather than an exhaustive systematic review. We organize the field using five dimensions: interaction paradigm, computational architecture, deployment form, orchestration mode, and human-oversight mode. Treating oversight separately from architecture resolves a conceptual overlap in earlier classifications and gives each representative system one value per dimension. The technical synthesis covers repository context, planning, tool use, multi-agent coordination, SDLC applications, and benchmark limitations. We keep technical capability evidence separate from business and adoption reports. Vendor and news sources are used as dated context, not as proxies for maturity or user preference. The survey covers material available through 28 February 2026.

papers.title: Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
papers.summary: Automation platforms such as GitHub Actions and n8n are increasingly adopting so-called agentic workflows, which integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents for tasks such as code review and data synchronization. While bringing convenience for developers, this integration exposes a new risk: An adversary may control and craft certain inputs, such as GitHub issue comments, to manipulate the LLM agent for unwanted actions, such as credential exfiltration and arbitrary command execution. To our knowledge, no prior academic work has studied such a risk in agentic workflows. In this paper, we design the first detection and exploitation framework, called JAW, to hijack agentic workflows hosted on automation platforms via a novel approach called Context-Grounded Evolution. Our key idea is to evolve agentic workflow inputs under the contexts derived from hybrid program analysis for hijacking purposes. Specifically, JAW generates agentic workflow contexts through three analyses: (i) static path-feasibility analysis to identify feasible agent-invocation paths and the input constraints required to trigger them, (ii) dynamic prompt-provenance analysis to determine how that input is transformed and embedded into the LLM context, and (iii) capability analysis to identify the actions and restrictions available to the agent at runtime. Our evaluation of JAW on GitHub workflows and n8n template

papers.title: What makes an LLM a tutor? A component-centric survey of LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems
papers.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation. We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy

papers.title: When to Delegate: A Measurement Study of Bounded Agent Teams for Personal Super Agents
papers.summary: Abstract Personal super agents coordinate many tools while remaining fast, safe, and accountable to one user. A popular design is a Router delegating to Workers. Recent work shows coordination can cost more than it returns, but transfer to personal agents—single-user context, side-effecting tools, cross-turn references, and refusals—is not established. We present the bounded-delegation runtime protocol, instantiate it in Eva, a 22-tool in-vehicle agent, and introduce Eva-Bench, 80 rule-scored tasks in ten categories. With one real model and tool set, we compare monolithic ReAct, bounded team, and unbounded team, and ablate budgets, reasoning, concurrency, guards, ledger, and injected failures. Delegation is not free: the main team pays 2.75×the latency and 2.59×the tokens. In one full-suite run it leads by one task (92.5% versus 91.2%), but three full-suite repetitions give 92.9% versus 93.3% (difference -0.4pp). Four post hoc temperature- matched runs average 90.6% (range 86.2–93.8%), so temperature alone does not explain the team’s small, unstable lead. We do not claim a general team advantage. The stable finding is the tax; service workflows and cross-turn references favor the team in repeated data, while safety and aggregate success do not. Bounded budgets reduce tail latency, reasoning is a net cost, and guards/ledger are null at oracle success. A selective-delegation poli

papers.title: Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Theory-Aligned Social Science Content Analysis: Evidence From Collaborative Learning Discourse
papers.summary: Theory-based content analysis is central to social science research, but coding context-dependent interactional discourse remains difficult to scale. This study examines whether fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) can support theory-aligned, episode-level coding of complex social interaction, using socially shared metacognitive regulation (SSMR) in collaborative learning discourse as a demanding empirical case. Using a human-coded dataset of 2,372 discourse episodes from undergraduate collaborative problem-solving, we adapted the large language model content analysis (LACA) framework through an AI-aligned codebook, prompt design, and supervised fine-tuning. Prompt-only and fine-tuned models were compared across episode-level classification and multilayer SSMR coding. Fine-tuned models substantially improved agreement with human coding and predictive performance relative to prompt-only baselines. Performance was strongest for episode-level classification and several higher-support coding layers, whereas errors remained concentrated in sparse, boundary-prone, and highly interpretive categories requiring social-intent reconstruction and temporally unfolding context. The findings extend recent work on LLM-assisted qualitative and content analysis by showing both the promise and limits of supervised, theory-aligned automation for multilayer social interaction coding. Overall, th

papers.title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human–Agent Interfaces
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). Our findings suggest that the primary benefit of human–agent i

papers.title: SoK: Sticky Policies Come Unstuck: Where Data-Governance Claims End at Generative Handoffs
papers.summary: Modern applications move data through databases, APIs, observability pipelines, and generative systems; each hop can create a new data object: a stored derivative, an agent's tool result, per-step logs. Each component may correctly enforce its controls while the end-to-end path loses the governance basis for new outputs. LLMs both ease and complicate this crossing: they interpret ordinary-language claims without the sender's executable policy grammar, yet create content probabilistically and may release it. We characterize data-governance preservation as an architectural property of generative paths under a declared scope and trust model. At each in-scope use or release, the responsible mechanism must identify the exact output's applicable claims, join them with current request authority, and mediate every declared path. After content-changing derivation, authorized transition semantics must establish the output's governance basis and make it obtainable or resolvable downstream. We formalize this as a decision-factorization condition: correctness is possible exactly when every trusted-state equivalence class retains a common permitted decision; no universal policy language is required. We evaluate sixteen mechanism families across six lifecycle stages and four cross-stage interfaces, and we adjudicate eight product- and protocol-specific boundary paths selected as the strongest

papers.title: Personas shift clinical action thresholds in large language models
papers.summary: Clinical large language model (LLM) deployment is shifting from feasibility to liability, while current guidance largely treats model behavior as a control problem. We tested whether decision-style system prompts shift clinical action thresholds when clinical facts are held constant, and whether these shifts are consistent across settings and models. We defined nine physician personas by crossing three ethical orientations (duty-based, care-based, utilitarian) with three cognitive styles (intuitive, integrative, analytic). Twenty open-weight LLMs were evaluated on 2500 simulated emergency department vignettes and 2500 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries. For each text, models answered five binary decision items (safety, autonomy, treatment, resource use, follow-up). Each condition was repeated ten times, yielding 5,000,000 total decisions. Under baseline prompting, models answered “Yes” to 42.8% of decisions. Persona prompts shifted affirmative rates from 36.9% to 46.4%, a 9.5 percentage-point swing under fixed clinical evidence. Effects were largest in autonomy and treatment and were consistent across corpora (85.7% directional agreement; r = 0.82 for effect sizes). Susceptibility varied by model (4.9–16.1 points), with no consistent protection from medical fine-tuning or model size. papers.title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a

papers.title: Sharing is caring: Attestable and Trusted Cloud Pipelines out of Distrustful Components
papers.summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) protect private memory and attest initial code and configuration, but neither constrain nor attest shared channels between TEEs or with the untrusted host. Confidentiality thus depends on the functional correctness of all in-TEE code accessing these channels: a single misuse can leak data and compromise a pipeline. This assumption is increasingly untenable for agentic applications that generate code at runtime and cloud pipelines of mutually distrustful components. We present MICA, a confidential-computing firmware extension that decouples confidentiality from trust in in-TEE code. MICA lets tenants define, restrict, and attest channel constraints between TEEs and with the untrusted host, including transitive constraints spanning a pipeline. It extends attestation to groups of communicating TEEs, letting external parties verify the confidentiality properties induced by these constraints across a pipeline. We implement MICA on Arm CCA by extending the Realm Management Monitor with a small policy language, requiring no hardware changes and minor QEMU and KVM changes. Our evaluation demonstrates support for confidential agentic applications and pipeline computations without trusting the functional correctness of in-TEE code. MICA increases the TCB by 7% and incurs infrequent setup costs: 2-4% boot-time overhead, approximately 1.5 s for policy

papers.title: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool calling to complete tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool calling between LLM agents and tool providers. It reduces integration cost and drives rapid growth in tool scale. In production deployments, tool access becomes difficult to scale. On the tool provider side, legacy services are not directly callable through MCP; the rapid protocol development creates ongoing compatibility cost. On the agent side, the number of mounted tools is limited by the LLM context window and inference overhead; mounting a large tool set increases token usage and inference latency and can reduce task success rate. Moreover, for stateful MCP backends with multiple replicas, preserving session affinity increases client-side complexity. We present a cloud-scale MCP Gateway system. It breaks the direct-connect model on the data plane and offloads legacy service integration, consolidating incompatible MCP variants, access control, tool recommendation, and session-aware routing at the gateway. The conversion module supports 315 OpenAPI services in the cloud and integrates MCP transport variants. Session-aware routing decouples the scalability of the gateway layer and the MCP service layer. The hybrid retrieval engine sustains $\sim$98\% Top-15 recall; it scales agent tool access to 3{,}000+ tools with improved tool selection accuracy. We also share the

papers.title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
papers.summary: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.

papers.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.

papers.title: SkillCODER: Towards Auditing and Attribution of Copyright Infringement in LLM Agent Skills
papers.summary: Agent skills package reusable workflows, constraints, and task-specific procedures into deployable text artifacts for LLM-based agent ecosystems. Unlike conventional system prompts, skills are distinguished by scale, spanning hundreds or thousands of tokens across many sections, and readability, being written in natural language. These properties make skills valuable but also vulnerable to copyright infringement: licensed buyers can redistribute a skill, and shared skills can be repackaged without consent. Existing copyright auditing methods for system prompts are inadequate here: skill length dilutes watermark signals, while their token-level perturbations compromise the readability essential to a skill's utility. We therefore propose SkillCODER, a method for copyright auditing and buyer attribution of agent skills under a practical black-box, content-only setting. SkillCODER operates in two phases. In the embedding phase, it parses the skill into a section-aware intermediate representation, SkillIR, that identifies stable structural anchors; it then embeds ownership evidence by distributing conditional instructions across structural nodes to form an Artifact-Gated Capsule, designed to activate under defender-designed verification queries and remain dormant otherwise; and it encodes a buyer-specific fingerprint via Controlled-Vocabulary Error-Correcting Codes that bind each co

Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Can TDD improve the quality of LLM-migrated code? : A pilot study in an industrial context
papers.summary: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLM) has created new possibilities for automating software development, yet ensuring the quality of AI-generated code remains a major challenge. We aim to investigate if Test-Driven Development (TDD) can improve the quality of code generated by an LLM in a fully autonomous context, within a pilot project at Decerno AB. We added TDD to their pilot workflow, using a design science approach, with continuous refinements to prompt design and workflow structure, based on observed AI behavior. The generated code was evaluated and compared with non-TDD code, using SonarQube for static code analysis. The results indicate that TDD reduced complexity and code duplication, but introduced more quality issues overall, while non-TDD produced fewer, but more severe issues. The generated tests from the TDD workflow focused more on content verification than on behavioral testing, contributing to a lower code coverage per test compared to non-TDD. The findings suggest that TDD involves trade-offs that may favor certain development priorities, in particular where lower complexity and reduced duplication are more beneficial than minimizing total issue count. This indicates that a strict application of TDD may not be optimal in an autonomous AI-driven context, and that exploring more flexible adaptations of the TDD workflow remains interesting for future resea

papers.title: From Coding to Creativity: Integrating Design Thinking into IT and Technology Education
papers.summary: This study examines how the integration of Design Thinking into Information Technology (IT) and technology education can bridge technical programming skills and creative, human-centered problem-solving. Specifically, it explores how the five stages of Design Thinking empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, and testing shape students’ creative thinking, active engagement, and collaborative learning experiences. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving teachers, students, and school principals as key informants. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of learning activities, then analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns in teaching practices and student experiences. The findings indicate that Design Thinking creates opportunities for students to move beyond coding procedures toward developing digital solutions that respond to real users’ needs. Through collaborative ideation, iterative prototyping, and feedback-based testing, students demonstrate greater involvement in learning, explore alternative solutions, and communicate their ideas more actively. The approach also provides opportunities to develop empathy, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to experiment with and revise initial designs. Meanwhile, teachers assume a facilitative role by guiding inquiry, supporting experimentation, an

papers.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly ‘reason’ with increasing sophistication, but whether they ‘know’ when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning–Kruger–like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence–accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning syst

papers.title: Machine thinking and the human mind
papers.summary: Abstract This opinion article examines the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence by contrasting human intelligence with machine capabilities across physical, perceptual, cognitive, metacognitive, and social dimensions. As AI shifts from narrow task‐oriented models to general‐purpose agents and autonomous systems, the article addresses critical technical and existential challenges, including model hallucinations, opaque capabilities, and skills displacement. To ensure AI is safe and beneficial alignment with human interests, it advocates moving beyond conventional post‐training techniques toward objective‐driven architectures grounded in self‐awareness, metacognition, and human values. Ultimately, the piece calls for reorienting education and society to cultivate the human mind—fostering ethical, compassionate polymaths capable of thriving alongside advanced machine intelligence.

papers.title: Advancing Learner Autonomy in Adult Online Education: An Evidence-Based Framework for Practice
papers.summary: Online learning in higher education continues to expand, but persistent challenges of student isolation, disconnection, and retention require innovative engagement strategies. Self-regulation and autonomy play a critical role, and the ability to develop skills in planning, managing, and controlling their learning behaviors is critical to student success. Engagement is widely recognized as essential for learner satisfaction and course completion, and research consistently indicates a clear link between instructor engagement, learner engagement, and actual learning. Successful on-ground instruction does not always translate to successful online instruction, and facilitators require appropriate professional development related to online delivery and methodologies. Ensuring online learner success requires a combination of intentional course design, proactive support, and the cultivation of learner self-regulation skills. To facilitate persistence and understand and effectively address the multiple needs of a diverse adult learner population, instructors must implement andragogical strategies that will keep learners motivated and actively engaged. Heutagogy is of particular interest to adult online education, which shares key attributes with it, such as learner autonomy and self-direction, and has roots in adult teaching and learning. This article explores the application of theory

papers.title: TurboRetry: Mitigating Large-Scale QUIC Handshake Floods with Off-the-Shelf DPU Offloading
papers.summary: The modern transport protocol QUIC is designed to enhance network performance and security, but it remains vulnerable to handshake flooding attacks. Such attacks exhaust CPU resources by forcing the server to perform expensive cryptographic operations via a large number of handshaking requests. QUIC provides a built-in defense mechanism, the Retry mechanism, to mitigate these attacks. However, our experiments reveal that it can still become a performance bottleneck under large-scale QUIC handshake floods due to substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we design and implement TurboRetry, a split design, that offloads the Retry mechanism onto DPUs to efficiently mitigate QUIC handshake floods. TurboRetry partitions the tasks of the Retry into two categories, and then assigns them to the DPUs and the host, respectively. To preserve QUIC semantics and reduce the coordination overhead, TurboRetry designs an extended Retry token format and an efficient cooperation scheme. In addition, TurboRetry offloads the connection authorization task to the on-path Data Path Accelerator (DPA) to further improve both performance and security. Our evaluation shows that TurboRetry increases the maximum sustainable attack rate by 10--20× over host QUIC stacks.

papers.title: Investigating the association between problematic social media use and the feeling of self-alienation.

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: An Assessment of Accessibility and Affordability of Inpatient Psychiatric Care in Tennessee
papers.summary: Introduction: Access to mental health has seen changes over the past decade, but little research and attention have been given to access to inpatient psychiatric facilities. Inpatient psychiatric care is crucial for patients experiencing mental health emergencies who need immediate access to care. Gaps in spatial accessibility, affordability, and the access and assessment process were identified due to a lack of available information in the field. Methods: Secondary data from the Tennessee Department of Health were used to assess financial accessibility through payer source charges and patient encounters, as well as through mapping of inpatient psychiatric facilities and conducting drive time and coverage area analyses. Primary data were collected through interviews with clinicians located in Northeastern Tennessee to gain insight into the assessment process and gather their perceptions of inpatient care. Results: Longitudinal descriptive reviews on the financial accessibility among Tennessee Inpatient Facilities. This showed increased variability among facilities when stratified by region, ownership, and type of operation. Spatial accessibility in ArcGIS showed 82% of counties were not covered within a 30-minute radius of inpatient facilities. Analysis showed that Middle Tennessee had significantly less coverage from inpatient facilities and raised concerns about spatial-socia

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Sex-Dependent Modulation of the Endocannabinoid System in Pain Processing
papers.summary: Medical cannabis, also known as medical marijuana, is becoming a more popular treatment for many diseases, including chronic pain. Chronic pain is difficult to treat, and current pain relievers are less effective in women. Medical cannabis may be a useful alternative to the medications that are currently available, but more research is needed to determine how safe and effective it is. Cannabis belongs to a class of drugs known as cannabinoids, which act on the body’s own endocannabinoid system to produce its effects. Cannabinoids affect the sexes differently, but it is not clear what causes these differences. Our research explored how sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone affect the efficacy of cannabinoids. To do this, I first examined whether removing these hormones would affect the brain’s response to THC, the main ingredient in cannabis. I found that THC affected brain regions differently in mice with depleted hormones. Additionally, THC affected brain regions differently in males and females. Next, I tested whether testosterone and estrogen affected how well cannabinoids worked as pain relievers. I found that testosterone reduced the drug’s efficacy in females, while estrogens reduced its efficacy in males.
